analysis.one_liner: Funds a CDC program to stop teen e-cigarette and tobacco use through research and education.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have authorized $100 million a year for five years for a CDC initiative to reduce youth e-cigarette use, never received a vote after being referred to a House subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The PROTECT Act would have directed the CDC to run a program to prevent and reduce e-cigarette and other tobacco use among young people. It would have paid for research on products, usage patterns, and health effects; guidance for doctors and schools on helping young users quit; a national public education campaign; and continued grants to state and local health departments for tobacco control. It authorized $100 million per year for fiscal years 2022 through 2026.
analysis.who_benefits: Young people, who would benefit from federal research, education, and treatment programs aimed at keeping them off nicotine; schools and health care providers, who would get guidance on intervening with young users; and state, local, tribal, and territorial health departments, whose tobacco control programs would keep receiving grant funding. Families gain from reduced youth nicotine addiction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Young people at risk of nicotine addiction

how_it_helps.text: Directs the CDC to run a Reducing Youth Use of E-Cigarettes Initiative, including research on products, usage patterns, dependence, and the marketing strategies manufacturers use to reach young people.

Requires guidance for health care providers, schools, and others on intervening with and treating young people who use e-cigarettes, and work on cessation strategies and quit support designed for youth and young adults.
Mandates a national public education campaign, coordinated with the Surgeon General, on the harms of youth e-cigarette use and how to intervene.
Continues CDC grant funding to state, local, territorial, island, and tribal health departments for tobacco control and youth cessation services.
Authorizes $100,000,000 in appropriations for each of fiscal years 2022 through 2026 to carry out the initiative.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the $100 million annual appropriation; the tobacco and e-cigarette industries could face greater public scrutiny of their products and marketing, though the bill imposes no new bans, taxes, or product restrictions.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds $500 million in new federal spending over five years and does not itself restrict the sale, flavoring, or marketing of e-cigarettes, so critics could argue it funds research and education without directly limiting youth access to the products.

The Secretary must ensure the initiative does not duplicate other HHS activities, and much of the CDC's existing youth tobacco surveillance and education work overlaps with what the bill authorizes, raising questions about how much is genuinely new.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest, targeted public-health investment: roughly $100 million a year for research, education, and state grants aimed at reducing youth nicotine addiction. The cost to taxpayers is small by federal standards, and the bill avoids imposing new mandates on consumers or businesses, though it also stops short of direct product restrictions that some advocates wanted. Its main weakness is that education and research do not by themselves keep e-cigarettes out of teenagers' hands.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a markup or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz introduced the PROTECT Act on October 8, 2021, with 14 Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and, three days later, to its Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was taken: the subcommittee never advanced the bill, and it received no markup or vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo prevailed. Manufacturers of e-cigarettes and other tobacco products avoided the added federal research, surveillance, and public education that would have scrutinized their products and marketing to young people, and no industry money was put at risk. Young people and public health programs gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: E-cigarette and tobacco manufacturers; status quo held

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out or scheduled a markup.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health
against.role: House Energy and Commerce subcommittee; held the bill until the Congress ended
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 11, 2021, and took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the bill's floor support is unknown; its sponsor and all 14 cosponsors were Democrats, but a Democratic-controlled House never moved it.

industries.note: The bill would have funded CDC research specifically into the products, flavors, marketing channels, and advertising strategies used to reach young users, plus a national campaign on the harms of youth vaping. It imposes no new bans or taxes, but it would have sharply increased public scrutiny of how these companies market to teenagers.

The bill researches links between youth e-cigarette use and smoking initiation and funds state tobacco control programs, which works against the industry's interest in new young customers. However, it creates no new product restrictions or excise taxes.

industries.industry: State, local, and tribal health departments
industries.note: The bill continues CDC grant funding for their tobacco control programs, including youth prevention and cessation work. Their interest runs alongside the public's.
